title: Ten Promises for Jerusalem: Fasts Become Feasts
summary: In a series of short oracles, nearly all introduced by the words this is what the LORD of Hosts says, God promises to return to Zion and make Jerusalem the City of Truth, filled with old people and playing children, and to gather his scattered people. He calls the builders to be strong, commands truth and justice, and declares that the mourning fasts will become joyful feasts. The chapter ends with the nations streaming to Jerusalem, and ten men from every language grasping the robe of a Jew because they have heard that God is with his people.
story: Chapter 7 looked back at the fathers' refusal and the exile it caused. Chapter 8 looks forward. The same God who scattered his people with a whirlwind now says he has resolved to do good to Jerusalem (verse 15). The chapter completes the answer to the delegation from Bethel (7:2-3), which asked whether to keep fasting: the fasts will become feasts. It also closes the first half of the book on a high note, gathering up the promises of the visions (God's jealous love, his return, his dwelling in Zion, the nations joining him) and handing them to a people who were still working on a half-finished temple in a nearly empty city.
historical:
The chapter continues the message dated to December 518 BC (7:1). Jerusalem at this time had a small population, and the surrounding towns were thinly settled; when Nehemiah arrived some seventy years later, he still found the city large and spacious but with few people in it (Nehemiah 7:4). The promise of old people sitting in the streets and children playing (verses 4-5) spoke to a community that had lost a generation to war, famine, and deportation.

Verse 9 refers to the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid, meaning Haggai and Zechariah in 520 BC (Haggai 2:18; Ezra 5:1-2). Verse 10 recalls the hardships before that day, when there were no wages, no safety, and neighbor turned against neighbor, conditions Haggai also describes (Haggai 1:6; 2:15-17). Verse 19 names four fasts: the fourth month recalled the breach of Jerusalem's walls in 587 or 586 BC (Jeremiah 39:2; 52:6-7), the fifth the burning of the temple, the seventh the murder of Gedaliah, and the tenth the beginning of the Babylonian siege (2 Kings 25:1).
cultural:
The picture of a good city in verses 4-5 is drawn from ordinary life. The streets and squares of an ancient town, near the gate, were where people met, traded, held court, and passed the time; old men and women sitting there with their staffs and children playing around them was a picture of peace, long life, and a secure future. The gates in verse 16 were where local elders heard cases and gave judgments (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-11), so true and sound judgments in your gates means honest local courts.

The robe of verse 23 translates a word that means the edge, corner, or hem of a garment. Israelites were commanded to wear tassels on the corners of their garments as reminders of God's commands (Numbers 15:38-40). To grasp someone's garment was a gesture of earnest appeal or of attaching oneself to that person (1 Samuel 15:27). Ten is a round number for a large group, and every tongue means every language, so the picture is of many people from many nations holding on to a single Jew. The word for Jew here, yehudi, originally meant a Judean, and by this period it was becoming the common name for the people of Israel as a whole.
literary: The chapter is built from ten short oracles, each beginning with the formula this is what the LORD says, nearly always with the title of Hosts (verses 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 19, 20, and 23). The number ten may be deliberate, an answer to ten words of promise matching the Ten Commandments or simply a sign of completeness. The chapter reverses the language of chapter 7: there God scattered his people, here he gathers them; there the land became a desolation, here the vine and the ground yield their fruit; there they were a curse, here they will be a blessing. The command let your hands be strong frames verses 9-13. The ethical commands of verses 16-17 repeat those of 7:9-10, showing that the promises do not replace the demand for justice.

outline.t: God returns to Zion: the City of Truth, old and young, gathered people
Let your hands be strong: from curse to blessing
God resolves to do good; speak truth and judge justly
The nations seek the LORD in Jerusalem

doctrines.note: The chapter pictures the future God has resolved to give: a city of truth, holiness, long life, children, harvests, and joy. What seems impossible to the remnant is not impossible to God (verse 6). Hope rests on his character and resolve, not on present circumstances.

They will be my people, and I will be their God (verse 8) is the core formula of God's covenant with Israel, repeated from Exodus to Jeremiah. After the exile seemed to break it, God reaffirms it in faithfulness and righteousness.
The chapter ends with the nations coming to seek the LORD because they have heard that God is with his people. Israel's life under God's blessing is itself a witness that draws others to him.

words.note: Qinah, jealousy or zeal. Verse 2 repeats it with emphasis, jealous with great zeal, jealous with great fervor. It is the protective passion of God's love for his people, the same word used in 1:14, now the foundation of every promise in the chapter.

Pala, to be wonderful, extraordinary, or too hard. Verse 6 asks if the promise seems impossible to the remnant, should it seem impossible to God? The same word appears in Genesis 18:14, when God asks Abraham whether anything is too hard for the LORD.

Emet, truth or faithfulness, what is firm and reliable. Jerusalem will be called the City of Truth (verse 3), its people must speak truth to one another and give true judgments (verse 16), and they are to love truth and peace (verse 19). The city's new name is also its calling.

Berakhah, blessing. Verse 13 reverses Israel's reputation: they had been a curse among the nations, a byword for disaster, and now they will be a blessing, echoing God's promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:2-3).

christ: Several threads in this chapter reach toward the New Testament. Paul quotes the command of verse 16 when he tells the church to put off falsehood and speak truthfully to one's neighbor, since we are members of one another (Ephesians 4:25). The promise that fasts will become feasts matches Jesus's saying that the guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them (Mark 2:19). The closing picture of Gentiles grasping the robe of a Jew because God is with him finds a striking echo in the Gospels, where people reached out to touch the edge of Jesus's garment to be healed (Matthew 9:20; 14:36), and in the gathering of the nations to Israel's Messiah after the resurrection. The promise that God will dwell in Jerusalem and gather his people from east and west recalls Jesus's own words that many will come from east and west to recline at table in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11). These are echoes and fulfillments of a shared hope rather than direct predictions.
questions: Old people in the streets and children playing: why do you think God chose such ordinary pictures to describe his restored city?
The commands to speak truth and judge justly come right after the promises. How do God's promises and his commands work together?
The nations came because they heard that God was with his people. What would make others say that of your church or community?
